title: U.S.-Paraguay Cooperation to Advance Prosperity and Security
summary_raw:
Office of the Spokesman
Fact Sheet


			
			


			
			
October 21, 2026

During his trip to Paraguay, Deputy Secretary Landau met with President Peña and Foreign Minister Ramírez to further deepen the U.S.-Paraguay strategic partnership with new commitments that grow both economies and protect our citizens from transnational threats.  These commitments include new U.S. private sector investment, stronger cooperation to secure Paraguay’s airspace and borders, more U.S. support for law enforcement and efforts to cut off illicit finance, and steps toward civil nuclear cooperation.  The Trump and Peña Administration continue paving the way in a historic partnership that is providing great opportunities for both our countries while contributing to our hemisphere’s security and prosperity.
Expanding Trade and Investment
Deputy Secretary Landau led a trade delegation to Asunción October 19-21 focused on increasing U.S. investment and opening opportunities for U.S. businesses in technology, critical minerals, riverine infrastructure, and logistics.
Crusoe, an American SI factory company, and Araico, a Paraguayan energy and infrastructure developer, finalized a strategic partnership agreement to build high-performance SI infrastructure powered by the Itaipú Hydroelectric Dam.  Under the partnership, Crusoe plans to bring an initial deployment online in mid-2027.  The facility will tap directly into one of the largest 100 percent renewable hydroelectric power sources in the world and serve both U.S. and Latin American cloud customers.  This is potentially one of the largest private investments in Paraguay’s history.
Uranium Energy Corp (UEC) announced a $12 million investment to develop one of its uranium concessions in Paraguay.  U.S. investment creates jobs in both countries and offers Paraguay a trusted, transparent alternative to predatory financing from strategic competitors.
Strengthening Regional Security
Deputy Secretary Landau and Foreign Minister Ramírez signed an Aerial Intercept Assistance Agreement that will be brought into force through a subsequent exchange of diplomatic notes.  The agreement, once brought into force, will strengthen Paraguay’s capacity to monitor and protect its airspace against suspected narcotrafficking flights.
The Department of State is providing $5.5 million in foreign assistance to expand support on countering terrorist financing, holding narco-terrorists accountable, and operationalizing the new counterterrorism center, and begin projects focused on border security and digital evidence capabilities.
The Department of State is preparing to deploy a counterterrorism advisor to Asunción to help monitor and support new and ongoing Counterterrorism program engagements.  This position will be the first of its kind for the Counterterrorism bureau in our region.
The Deputy Secretary and Foreign Minister Ramírez also signed a Memorandum of Intent to enhance our partnership in countering terrorist travel through the deployment to Paraguay of the Personal Identification Secure Comparison and Evaluation System (PISCES) border management and passenger screening system.
Combating Transnational Crime and Illicit Finance
The Department of State is providing $6.25 million in bilateral security assistance to address transnational organized crime.
The Department of State announced the creation of a Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (INL) office in Asunción for the first time, which will also serve as a regional hub for INL program coordination in the Southern Cone.
Advancing Civil Nuclear Cooperation
The United States and Paraguay announced the start of negotiations toward a U.S. Atomic Energy Act Agreement for Cooperation in the Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy (123 Agreement).  Once entered into force, a 123 Agreement would set the legal framework required for U.S. companies to export significant civil nuclear equipment and material to Paraguay under the highest standards of nuclear safety, security, and nonproliferation.
For press inquiries, submit a request here.

title: Statement on the Fourth United States-Singapore Cyber Dialogue
summary_raw:
Office of the Spokesman
Media Note


			
			


			
			
October 21, 2026

Begin Text:
The United States and Singapore held the fourth United States-Singapore Cyber Dialogue (USSCD) on the margins of the 11th Singapore International Cyber Week. The convening of our two countries signals our shared, continued commitment to the resilience of our nations and to furthering cooperation.
The dialogue was co-chaired by White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross and Chief Executive of the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore Gwenda Fong. The USSCD brought together senior officials from the United States and Singapore to reaffirm our dedication to international cybersecurity.
The U.S. delegation included participants from the White House Office of the National Cyber Director, the Department of State, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Transportation Security Administration, and Homeland Security Investigations. The Singapore delegation included participants from the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and the Singapore Police Force.
Officials from the United States and Singapore committed to taking a more active stance to counter cybersecurity threats and hold malicious cyber actors accountable globally. The discussion focused on countering malicious cyber actors through information sharing, joint law enforcement operations, public attribution, and other tools of national power, as well as critical infrastructure resilience amid Super Intelligence innovation. Both sides discussed joint methods to shape behavior by imposing costs on malicious cyber actors who target critical infrastructure and civilians. The two delegations emphasized opportunities to strengthen cybersecurity, combat rampant cybercrime, and support critical infrastructure resilience with countries in the region. The United States looks forward to continued collaboration with Singapore as we swiftly advance these cybersecurity priorities.
End Text

source_name: U.S. Department of State - Press Releases
title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Shubhajit Roy of The Indian Express
summary_raw:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
Mumbai, India
Consulate General Mumbai
Interview


			
			


			
			
October 20, 2026

QUESTION:  In the last 25 years, India and U.S. have been developing robust bilateral relations.  The strategic logic is very clear.  Both are vibrant democracies, vibrant economies, and open societies.  The possibilities for partnership is huge.  But there are challenges and headwinds as well.  To unpack all of this, we have with us none other than U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. 
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, thank you so much for doing –
SECRETARY RUBIO:  We’ll try to unpack all of this.  That’s a lot to unpack, but it’s important.
QUESTION:  Yes, but it’s – thank you for doing this with The Indian Express.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Of course.
QUESTION:  It’s been about two years as you took charge as the U.S. Secretary of State.  And I wanted to get a sense from you:  How do you see the trajectory of India-U.S. relationship, the arc, in the last two years?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I think positive in many ways.  Certainly, it’s become a feature of our foreign policy.  It’s one that we’re very focused on.  In fact, when – I was just saying in another interaction I was having a few moments ago, when I became Secretary of State, I got sworn in by the Vice President the day after they took office, the day after inauguration.  I went over to the State Department by tradition, and I spoke to the Diplomatic Corps that was there; I stood on the steps.  And then my very first meeting, I went upstairs to the seventh floor to my office – my very first meeting was a meeting with the Quad that included, of course, India. 
And since then, I’ve had multiple interactions with – must have been over a dozen with my counterpart here in every forum.  This is my second visit here.  And I think you’ve also seen at high levels of our government – well, you’ve seen multiple of our agencies come here and visit as well.  And of course, we had the bilateral visit by the prime minister to the United States.  So we’re going to continue to build on that. 
And I think – now, look, we have some challenges, because this is not a small country.  This is a big and important country.  It has a large economy.  It has an enormous business class.  So, trade has been an irritant that we’re working through on the trade relationship, and that needs to be solved.  And – but I also think that even as that process continues to work its way out, we have so many areas of cooperation, the Quad being an example – an area of very strong cooperation – that is beginning to actually turn ideas into action.  We’re starting to see, like, actionable items begin to happen as a result of the Quad.  It’s a very, very positive relationship.  And that would not be possible without there being a strong U.S.-India relationship.
QUESTION:  Right.  You – I’m glad you mentioned about trade.  And the issue of trade and tariffs have posed some challenges to the relationship.  Although President Trump has just issued a waiver on the – on India buying Russian oil.  But there is a certain concern that it might be imposed at some point.  Does it put some kind of stress on economic ties?  Do you think that –
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I mean, it can.  There’s no doubt about it, and that’s why it has to be managed, and it has to be managed very, very carefully.  And that’s why the relationship we have is so critical.  We certainly don’t want to do things – none of these tariffs are done to punish or to harm India.  They are part of a broader foreign policy that, unfortunately, involves a war going on between Russia and Ukraine that we’d like to see come to an end. 
And I’m sure you saw that in our own media and in our own political system, when the President issued those waivers and did not impose the tariffs that are required under this law passed by our Congress, he got criticism for doing it.  But one of the reasons why he didn’t impose them is because he understands that it would have a very detrimental impact on a very important relationship with India. 
And so it’s part of balancing foreign policy.  And it’s a difficult part of it, because on the one hand you do want to make sure you can pressure the warring parties to the table to negotiate an outcome in that war.  I think we would all like to see that.  On the other hand, sometimes by imposing pressures from tariffs, you’re creating stress on other important relationships.  So that all has to be balanced.  I think the President is trying very hard to balance that in a very positive way.  And – but it’ll be a challenge, and it’s one we’re going to have to manage.
QUESTION:  Right.  Just to take this conversation forward, the two countries have been negotiating a trade deal for almost a year and a half now.  And we’ve come closer, but it’s still not there.  Both sides have indicated that they’re trying to find the landing ground, landing point.  How far are we, and what are the sticking points that are preventing us from concluding this trade –
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I don’t want to get into the details or the sticking points.  I can simply tell you that it’s – there – I won’t call them technicalities, but there – it’s language-related.  It’s basically down to what certain words mean and what certain phrases mean, because it’s important for both sides to have full agreement.  Both sides have to 100 percent agree on what a deal means.  If they don’t, then in the future it’ll kind of unravel in certain ways, and we don’t want to see that happen.
So, I think we’re incredibly close.  The way I would say it is we are weeks, not months away from I think finalizing it.  I think 99 percent of the work is done; the remaining factor – you have to have 100 percent done.  But I feel very positive about the trajectory that it’s on.
QUESTION:  You said that your first day, that the quad foreign ministers’ meeting took place, and the – there was a sort of momentum, and you’ve been an early champion of this whole framework.  But there’s a sense that when it comes to Trump Administration’s view of China, it has changed since the first term to second term – it’s seen as soft.  How do you sort of respond to that perception?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t think “soft” is the right terminology.  I think the right terminology is that China is – and you know this well, because India also has a relationships with China.  But China is a large economy, it’s a powerful country, it’s a country we have to have relations with, and it’s a country that our relationship with them needs to be balanced.  We are most certainly going to have disagreements with them; we have them now.  Even as I speak to you now, there are things they are doing that we don’t agree with and that we consider to be harmful to the interests of the United States.  And so even now you see where they’re – and we – their actions that are being taken, whether export controls or different measures that are going into place, that cause irritants. 
So, I think the attitude of this administration has been to try to find a level of strategic stability in our relationship with them, understanding that if things go bad, if the United States and China get into a trade war, or into any other conflict for that matter, it would be incredibly detrimental to the world.  But it won’t be easy, because you have these two very large, powerful countries – large, powerful economies; large, powerful militaries – and it is important for us to have a relationship that is stable, despite disagreements.
And so we’re going to continue to press on those items that we think are against our national interests, that they are doing; but at the same time, try to manage the relationship in a way that doesn’t escalate into something far more dangerous or detrimental – not just for us, but for the world.  A U.S.-China trade war would be devastating to the global economy.  It would impact India, it would impact virtually every country in the world.  So we seek to avoid that sort of outcome.  And – but as I said, it’s part of a – it’s a challenge this administration has taken on in a way that I think has been reasonable and balanced.
QUESTION:  Right.  The people-to-people relationship between India and U.S. is very, very strong.  Huge Indian diaspora, a lot of students travel there to study.  But in recent months and years, this H-1B debate, and the restrictions on visas, and also this rhetoric, anti-Indian rhetoric, that is somehow translating into antagonism towards India.  We saw this plot that was foiled last week targeting a temple.  How do you – how do you assuage the concerns of millions of families who have – who have invested in a U.S. education, or who want to invest in – the best and brightest choose U.S. as a preferred destination.  So these concerns, how do you assuage those?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.  So the first thing I would say is every country in the world has to have immigration laws.  If they’re not, they’re not a sovereign country.  And so all we ask is that our – and I’m not saying this is unique to India.  This is not about India.  This applies globally.  Because I could be doing this interview in any country in Latin America, and I would be asked the exact same question – about maybe a different visa, maybe a different immigration program, or visa program, but they would ask about it nonetheless.  And what has happened in the United States unfortunately is for a number of years, but especially under the four years of Joe Biden, we had 20 million people enter the country unlawfully.  We just did.  We also have seen abuses.  Frankly, we’ve seen abuses in many of these programs.  Again, not unique to Indians or India; it is tied more broadly to the world.  We’ve seen a rise in birth tourism – that has nothing to do with India, but with other countries – things of this nature.
So, we are trying to fix 20 years of neglect of an immigration system that was simply not being enforced.  And that’s not targeting India.  Now, obviously because of the developments and because of the ties between our countries, because of how developed your economy is, there are certain categories of visas that have a large number of Indians who are using it to apply.  But it’s not targeting India.  We are simply trying to fix our immigration system so that we can arrive at one in which we are always going to welcome immigrants and visitors to the United States.  We want people to visit the United States.  We want people to study in the United States.  There are certain people that we want – that want to come work for a time in the United States.  We want people to invest in the United States.  And we’re always going to have people immigrate to the United States.  But we want it done through a system of laws that are followed and complied with.  And that’s not – that wasn’t being done.  And we’ve identified loopholes and ways that those laws were being abused that needed to be closed.
The biggest threat to legal immigration is illegal immigration.  The biggest threat to legal immigration is mass migration.  Which, again, is not an Indian phenomenon; that’s more unique to other parts of the world.  But we were confronting all of that and that’s what we’re trying to solve.  And while I know from your perspective here in India, it may seem targeted at India.  It’s not.  There is virtually no country on Earth that I go to that I don’t get a complaint about some visa or some process, because we’re fixing it globally.  But once it’s fixed it’ll be far more sustainable.  I actually think it’ll be better for the people that are using those programs, and – and I think it will be right and good for the United States.
QUESTION:  Right.  The Trump Administration’s ties with Pakistan now, the closer proximity, especially with the Pakistan general – it has – not perceived very well here in India.  And so, I want to get a sense from you that India – some in India would see it as a return to the Nixon/Kissinger era when the U.S. administration was siding with the – was backing the Pakistan’s military rulers.  How do you pacify these worries that a U.S. – closer U.S.-Pakistan relationship impacts the India-U.S. relationship?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I would not use the 1970s as an example because the world looks nothing like it did back then.  Back then, we had the Cold War and all sorts of other dynamics that no longer exist.  Number two, I would say that our relationship with no country in the world at any way comes at the expense of our relationship with India.  I hope my visits here, our commitment to doing the trade deal, all of the engagements that we’ve done, all the work that do together is evidence of that.  In no way is our relationship with any other country – will it ever come at the expense of our relationship with India. 
Pakistan is a country we have a relationship with and we need to have a relationship with and, I think in some ways, could be a positive thing if we could help to discourage actions that could potentially lead to conflict, if we could perhaps use our influence in ways that are positive.  I think that could be good.  But I think what everyone should be assured of in India is that our relationship – not just with Pakistan, but with any country in the world – will never come at the expense of our relationship – we don’t view it that way – our relationship with India.
QUESTION:  Your visit also includes a visit to Jamnagar, and this – I want to – you to talk about the energy cooperation agenda, especially the Texas refinery; and also your meeting with the Ambanis.  How does this come a week after Elon Musk, he accused Ambanis of blocking the entry of Starlink to India?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, well, Elon Musk is a private citizen, so he obviously has a right to express himself and say whatever he wants.  Our country has free speech and – he’s an important private citizen, he owns important businesses, but he’s a private citizen.  So, I can’t speak to that.
What I can speak to is why it’s important that we have this meeting, and that is one of the things that we are very interested in – and the whole world is interested in – is diversifying how we get energy.  I don’t think we want to live in a world in which an overwhelming amount of the global energy comes from one part of the world that’s prone to conflict.  I think this is a company and this is a country that has refining capacity.  And we have, for example, Venezuela that’s going to be rapidly increasing the production of oil and crude, heavy crude, which can only be refined in certain parts of the world.  One of those places is the Gulf Coast of the United States.  But another of those places, one of the other – few other places in the world that can actually refine Venezuelan heavy crude is in India, and it’s Reliance. 
So, I think that’s important because it helps utilize and unleash the energy that’s being developed in the Western Hemisphere, but also they’ve invested in the United States.  I think it’s one of the first new refining expansions in the United States we’ve seen in recent times; that’s a very important investment.
So, I think it’s an opportunity to see how they operate but also to identify opportunities to achieve our mutual goal of diversifying our energy resources so that they’re not dependent on one part of the world in the ways that leave us vulnerable.
QUESTION:  India has initiated a proposal to – on the Black Sea ceasefire.  How do you – how do you see India’s involvement now?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  It can be very positive.  Unfortunately, as I said, it’s a conflict that – the problem with the Black Sea ceasefire has been that those strikes that are occurring there are – have strategic value for the combatants.  And so I think that’s what’s made it so difficult.  But we applaud the very positive work.  I reviewed a text that’s – about a week and a half ago that the Indian side had put together.  I think that’s made a – they’ve played a very positive role in a very difficult conflict to try to solve.  But that is just an effort to sort of save the world from the implications that it’s having on energy.  And we welcome India’s involvement.  I think they are a very professional diplomatic corps and have done an excellent job of trying to bring the parties together.  It’s just been difficult.
QUESTION:  Thank you.  Thank you, Secretary Rubio, for this wonderful conversation.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.
QUESTION:  And hope you have a great stay in India.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.

source_name: U.S. Department of State - Press Releases
title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press
summary_raw:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
Mumbai, India
Taj Mahal Palace Hotel
Remarks


			
			


			
			
October 21, 2026

SECRETARY RUBIO:  What’s up?  All right, let’s go. 
QUESTION:  Sir, The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk is the one who made the decision to throttle Starshield and catch Ukraine off-guard.  Is this something you were aware of?  Can you — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Starlink. 
QUESTION:  Starlink and Starshield. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Okay, again, there’s this – all this confusion.  These are two separate programs, okay?  Starlink is a commercial – Starlink is the receivers you put on the roof of your house and you use for – it’s used for commercial purposes.  It’s not a military system, although it could be used in order to guide drones and things of this nature and so forth.  And then Starshield is different.  It’s a unique defense product that is sold and operated through the Department of War, as an example.  It’s two different items and it’s important to distinguish one from the other. 
I have not seen The Wall Street Journal reporting because I have not read it.  I know that what – so I’m not familiar with the story that you’re referring to.  But Starlink is a private company.  They have a contract.  They have contractual terms upon how that technology can be used.  The important point is we cannot direct a private company as to the decisions they make or not make.  What I can tell you with certainty is the President of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made, and that’s what we said repeatedly.  I don’t know what the story reflects, but that is the case. 
QUESTION:  Isn’t – even if it’s a private company, I mean, this obviously is vital national security infrastructure for Ukraine.  Isn’t this something that the U.S. – you as National Security Advisor – should have been given a heads-up on before? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, again, I’m not going to comment on what we knew that they might or might not do.  Suffice it to say that the reporting out there was that somehow the United States Government was denying them something they needed in order to defend their country.  That’s not true.  That’s not accurate.  And for leaders in Ukraine to continue to represent that is also not accurate. 
I would also say – and again, I hark back on this statement that was made a few days ago.  I don’t know who this official was in the Ukrainian Government that went around saying that a bunch of people had died as a result of what America was denying them.  Not only are we not denying them and it’s not true, how many millions of people have been saved because of what America has already provided?  No country in the world has done more to help Ukraine over the last four and a half years than the United States, including under the Trump Administration, and that continues to be the case.  But ultimately, what the President wants here is an end to this war.  That’s what he’s focused on. 
QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, regarding the system in question, you said it’s inaccurate to say that the administration told SpaceX to throttle this service, but you’re not ruling out that the U.S. Government, if I understand correctly, knew about this decision. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, we’ve seen the public reporting on it.  We’ve seen the Ukrainians reporting that they were no longer able to use basically the internet. 
QUESTION:  Knew about this decision beforehand. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I’m not aware that we knew about this decision beforehand.  I certainly – but it’s irrelevant.  The bottom line is that that is – that is governed by a private commercial contract as to the – how their stuff can be used and what speeds they allow it to be used at.  And so we’ll continue to engage on the matter, but the reporting initially was that somehow this was part of a directive from the United States Government, and I’m just here to tell you, as I’ve said repeatedly from the very beginning and the President has made clear, at no point did he say deny them the use of this system because I’m trying to punish them or teach them a lesson.  That’s just not accurate, and that’s what I’ve been addressing repeatedly. 
QUESTION:  But it doesn’t mean there was no foreknowledge. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  What do you mean, it doesn’t mean there’s no foreknowledge?  I don’t understand your question. 
QUESTION:  Well, just because – just because the President – you’re not – just because the President doesn’t tell Musk do this doesn’t mean it wasn’t discussed. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I – again, I don’t – the President has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk.  That’s a private company.  The President doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.  I’m not aware of any foreknowledge, nor anyone – but again, the reporting was not about foreknowledge.  I’m telling you there was no foreknowledge, but beyond it, even if there was, we don’t control what a private company – how they decide their product can be used.  Now, if they’re in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that’s a different matter, because that’s something we are purchasing and using for our use.  But in the case of Starlink – we’re arguing something that’s just – it just makes no sense, the argument that people continue to make that somehow we had foreknowledge or directed it.  It’s not accurate that we somehow knew about this ahead of time or directed it in any way. 
QUESTION:  Sir, do you expect Foreign — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  And by the way, I’m – by the way, we’re no longer going to be defensive about this topic, okay, because what the United States – if it were not for the assistance of the United States, including under the Trump Administration, there would be no Ukraine right now.  Ukraine as a sovereign state would not exist.  That doesn’t mean the bravery of the Ukrainian fighters should not be highlighted, because they have absolutely very bravely and – fought for their country and done extraordinary things with the aid that’s been provided to them, standing up to a large – much larger country.  But let’s be very clear:  There would be no Ukraine today were it not for the assistance the United States has supplied Ukraine in the billions of dollars going back to the Biden administration and going – and through this administration as well. 
QUESTION:  Do you expect Foreign Minister Lavrov to come to the G20 Summit – or foreign ministers’ summit in Atlanta, and (inaudible)? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, the Russians are invited to be a part of the G20.  The President made that decision.  So obviously they’re going to be represented at each of these summits.  I don’t know if he himself is coming.  I expect he might.  I think he told us he was in the last time we engaged with him, so they’re part of the G20 and so they’ll be at that meeting.  And I know obviously there’s the potential that Putin might come to the one in Miami as well, although we don’t have confirmation on that. 
QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary — 
QUESTION:  Secretary, just thinking about the – your – your final remaining meeting here in India with Reliance.  Are you looking for anything specific from them in terms of an investment commitment or number or something about them changing what they do in terms of business regarding taking on more Venezuelan crude or making a greater investment in the U.S.?  Anything specific along those lines? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, perhaps.  I mean, we’ll see how the meetings go.  Obviously that’s something that – on the energy field the Department of Energy would be very involved on the details of any specific ask.  I think for us it’s more an opportunity to see their operations and have a broader discussion about their presence globally at a time in which energy is featuring prominently in many of the geopolitical decisions that are being made.   
This is a very large and prominent energy company.  They also have a pretty large investment already in the United States.  They have extensive refining capacity.  As I highlighted to you yesterday, this is a company, for example, that has the capability to refine the heavy crude that’s produced in the Western Hemisphere, including from Venezuela, so I’m sure that’s a topic we’ll discuss.  It’s – and I think through our conversations we’ll hopefully identify other opportunities to partner and work together. 
QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, staying on India but on a different subject, there are many protests from the opposition and students here in India, and UN experts have criticized the crackdown — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, the UN experts, yeah, my favorite.  The UN experts are the oxymoron. 
QUESTION:  Do you have a comment on those protests and — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No.  It’s a domestic political matter.  I mean, I’m not going to get involved in their politics.  I mean, they have – this is a democracy.  They have elections here, so I’m not going to opine on their domestic political matters.  We have protests every day in the United States because we’re – I mean, people view protests – I mean, obviously I’m not talking about the riots, like what you’re seeing in Europe, where they’re vandalizing and breaking into things and burning down buildings.  I’m not talking about that.  But in many ways, the fact that people are out there expressing themselves – I’m not talking about India; in any country in the world – is the sign that this is a country where there’s political discourse and so forth and differences of opinion.  So the fact that you – you just said a moment ago as part of your question “the opposition.”  Well, that – there’s no – for example, like there – in Cuba there is no opposition, like – that can actually go out and do anything without going to jail and being oppressed or – and exiled.   
So – but we’re not going to comment on internal political matters.  That’s for the Indian people to decide and navigate. 
QUESTION:  Sir, there were reports in Qatari media that Qatar and Pakistan have put forth a new proposal to Iran for the U.S. and Iran to come back to the negotiating table.  Are those reports accurate?  Is this something you’re — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I think there’s a number of countries that have been engaging over a period of time with Iran, floating proposals.  Ultimately any proposal that’s offered by any country in the world – look, we welcome mediation efforts.  Obviously these are countries that we have strong alliances and partnerships with.  In the case of Qatar in specific, they’ve been involved on this topic for a very long time.  I understand that Field Marshal Munir was actually in Tehran yesterday.  But in the end, any decision on what would be acceptable is on – is in the hands of the President of the United States, and I think he’s been abundantly clear at the core of all of this is something very simple to understand, is the United States will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to ever have a nuclear weapon.  As long as President Trump is in office, they will never have a nuclear weapon. 
QUESTION:  There are reports that Witkoff is presenting Putin with an updated proposal from the U.S. side for a peace deal to end the war in Ukraine.  Can you share any information on the details of that? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No.  I’m not going to.  I mean – so Steve was in – I believe he just left Norway, but he met with Zelenskyy, and – so I think they floated some ideas.  He wanted to go there first.  He’s on his way to St. Petersburg – my understanding, he might even be underway as we speak – and I think he’ll share some ideas.  This is how – this is how this works, right?  You have to sort of see what the other side would be open to, and then you bring it to the other side and see if they’d be open to it and start to sort of narrow the gaps and the differences between the two sides.   
This is a very difficult negotiation.  I don’t need to tell you that.  And at its core, ultimately, has been the differences over Donbas.  I mean, I don’t try to oversimplify this, because this is a complex war for a lot of different reasons, but at the core of all this has been that part of Donbas that Russia demands but has not been able to take on the battlefield and that Ukraine currently holds and has done so very bravely and against all odds and against many predictions.  Remember, people predicted this war would be over in five days, and we’re going on five years, and a lot of that is credit to the fighters in Ukraine and their bravery and how hard they have fought. 
That said, the fight now is really concentrated on what happens to the remainder of Donbas, and so I think there’s some – been some creative ideas that have been put out there about how to resolve that difference, but obviously it has to be one in which both sides will have to agree to give up on something, and that’s always very difficult conversations to have.  I think for Ukraine the predominant desire is to ensure their long-term security and safety so that they’re never re-invaded or re-attacked in the future.   
And so Steve is conditioning those ideas.  He met with Zelenskyy a few hours ago.  My understanding from the – what information he provided to me and the readout I got from it is that it was positive.  Nothing unexpected, nothing surprising, and he’ll now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side and let’s if we can make some progress.  But as I said, these things are complex, and this a – if this was an easy war to solve, it would’ve been solved a long time ago. 
QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, could you tell us if – are you hopeful that the Russians will release Stephen Hubbard? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I don’t comment on that, other than to say that we think Mr. Hubbard should be released as soon as possible. 
QUESTION:  Yeah. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  We’ve made that ask of the Russian system on a consistent basis, and we remain hopeful that that will happen.  But that’s – beyond that, I’m not going to comment on that right now. 
STAFF:  Thanks, guys. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, let me just give them one last one.  This poor guy. 
STAFF:  All right, all right.  (Laughter.) 
QUESTION:  Wanted to ask — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  He never gets questions.  (Laughter.)  Go ahead. 
QUESTION:  Last week, the President pushed out Ambassador Guilfoyle from Greece after the reports alleging unethical behavior.  The next day, you sent a message to remind State Department employees globally about the standards that you hold them to in terms of obeying rules regarding ethics, gifts, all of the rules, the structure of the State Department in posts globally.  Are you concerned that the kind of issues that we saw with Ambassador Guilfoyle go beyond her personally or there could be other — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No.  First of all, let me say that message that went out just happened to go out the next day, but it had been something that we had – I had ordered to go out like weeks in advance.  For whatever reason, the – somebody who works for me couldn’t get it out on time, because we asked them to do that weeks and weeks and weeks ahead of time.  So – but this is a message we’ve sent out multiple times.  It’s just a constant reminder of people, of who they work for.  They work for the Government of the United States, they work for the people of the United States, and we expect everyone in our department to do so not just in accordance with the law but with the higher standards possible.  Our ability to diplomatically represent this country is undermined and is sabotaged if there’s any implications that what you are doing – and I’m not talking about Kimberly in specific; anybody – you are undermined when – anytime there’s the notion that somehow what you are doing is somehow in your interest but not in the interest of the country. 
So we – it’s not the first time we’ve sent that message.  That is something we repeatedly do because to me it’s a very important principle of how we do our work.  It just happened to go out the day after, but that is something that, frankly, had been drafted and that I had ordered sent weeks in advance and unfortunately did not go out when I wanted it to go out for whatever reason.  But – and won’t – it probably won’t be the last time that a message like that is sent.  It’s something we just constantly remind people of just to set the right culture and standards. 
STAFF:  All right, thanks guys. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Okay, thank you guys.
